newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST - German rates to turn higher end-1997.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - German rates to turn higher end-1997.

text.p: The Bundesbank is likely to keep its famed steady hand on interest rates for another year, but its long-anticipated upward rate move will kick in around the end of 1997, analysts say.

A Reuters survey published on Wednesday polled 29 economists on their longterm rate views, and 13 said Germany's floor discount rate would rise to three percent in the last quarter of 1997, with six more seeing that level reached in early 1998.
All but two analysts said they expected the discount to rise off its current historic low of 2.50 percent by the third quarter of 1998.
The median forecast for the Lombard rate, the ceiling on German interest rates and now at 4.50 percent, predicted a rise to five percent in the first quarter of 1998.

"The Bundesbank's policy is really unusually expansive at the moment and there will come a time next year when this will have to be normalised," said Thomas Kull, economist at Westdeutsche Labndesbank in Duesseldorf.

The Bundesbank has kept its headline rates on hold since April, when it shaved 50 basis points off both. The move was viewed by many observers as the last major easing in the current cycle and as heralding the first German official rate rise since July 1992.

Analysts said an expected gradual recovery in the German economy, fueled in part by export demand, would finally prompt the Bundesbank to take action to curb any incipient inflationary tendencies toward the end of 1997.
"Inflation will be approaching the two percent level, that will be one of the main reasons," said Gerhard Grebe, economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.
"Growth is going to strengthen and long term rates will automatically start to rise," Grebe added.
Grebe himself, in line with the overall survey trend, predicts the discount and Lombard rates will rise to three percent and five percent respectively in the first quarter of 1998.

A parallel poll on expectations for German inflation showed that an average of 33 forecasts saw a gradual acceleration in consumer price growth to around two percent by the end of 1997. The Bundesbank is keen to keep inflation below two percent.
However economists also said that there was no need for urgent action on rates, since economic growth remained relatively sluggish.

The survey showed M3 money supply growth, the Bundesbank's main policy indicator, is expected to slow further in the year to come, although the growth will remain above the Bundesbank's target range of four to seven percent by the end of this year.

The median forcast for M3 throughout 1997 is six percent, after a gradual decline from 8.4 percent in September 1996, but growth was then seen accelerating slightly above six percent in the first half of 1998.

"We are still in a very stable environment so there is nothing there to force the Bundesbank to act quickly," said West LB's Kull, who sees the discount rate rising to three percent in the third quarter of 1997.

Kull predicted that the securities repurchase rate, now fixed at three percent, would move gradually upward to align more with the Lombard rate, and that the Bundesbank would eventually adjust its policy to reflect that.

"But these will be very slow moves. With the brake on budgetary policy at present, which will tend more to have negative consequences for the economy, there is no immediate need for the Bundesbank to tighten monetary policy as well," Kull added.
